lesson.title: Closing Politely: How TCP Connections End
lesson.summary: TCP termination closes each direction of a connection independently through an exchange of FIN and ACK segments, usually four segments but sometimes compressed to three, before either side discards its connection state.
lesson.body:
A TCP connection is really two independent byte streams layered on top of each other, one flowing from client to server and one from server to client, each with its own sequence numbering set up during the handshake. Because of that independence, closing a TCP connection is not a single farewell message, it is each direction being shut down on its own, using the FIN flag introduced back in the TCP segment header.

The typical pattern is often called a four way close, because it usually takes four segments to shut both directions down cleanly. Side A, having no more data to send, sends a segment with the FIN flag set. Side B acknowledges that FIN. At some point afterward, once side B has also finished sending its own data, side B sends its own FIN. Side A acknowledges that in turn. In the gap between side B acknowledging A's FIN and side B sending its own FIN, the connection is said to be half closed, side B can still send data to side A even though side A has already said it is done sending, precisely because the two directions close on separate schedules.

That four segment pattern is also sometimes compressed to three. If side B has no more data of its own to send and is ready to close immediately, it can combine its acknowledgment of side A's FIN with its own FIN into a single segment, often written as a FIN-ACK, the same way the handshake's second message combines an acknowledgment with a SYN into one SYN-ACK segment. So a real termination can show up as either four segments or three, depending on timing, and both are correct instances of the same underlying mechanism.

A worked example, continuing the numbers from the handshake, makes this concrete. Recall the handshake left the client's next byte to send at 1001 and the server's at 5001. Suppose the client sends a 500 byte request, bytes 1001 through 1500, the server fully replies, and both sides are now finished. The client, closing first, sends a FIN with sequence number 1501, since a FIN, like a SYN, consumes one sequence number of its own even though it carries no data. The server acknowledges with acknowledgment number 1502. Later, once the server has also finished sending its reply data and is ready to close, it sends its own FIN, and the client acknowledges that with acknowledgment number one greater than the server's FIN sequence number. At that point both directions are closed and the connection is fully torn down.

Two more details round this out. The side that sends the final acknowledgment, typically the side that closed first, enters a TIME_WAIT state for a period before fully discarding its connection state, usually set to twice the maximum time a segment could realistically still be wandering the network. This exists so that a stray, delayed duplicate segment from the old connection cannot be mistaken for part of a brand new connection that happens to reuse the same port pair shortly after. This graceful, negotiated close is also different from a reset: either side can send a segment with the RST flag at any point to abort a connection immediately, with no negotiation at all, typically used for error conditions such as trying to connect to a port nothing is listening on.
